lead: An avionics architecture is a plan of where computing happens and how data reaches the cockpit. Older aircraft use federated architecture: one box, one function. Newer aircraft use integrated modular avionics (IMA): a shared cabinet hosts several functions as separated software partitions. In both layouts the unit of design is the line replaceable unit (LRU), a box a technician can change on the flight line. This chapter compares the two layouts and then covers the built-in test equipment that keeps both of them maintainable.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for the platform types that shape these choices, and Chapter 4.7 for how the buses themselves work.

blocks.text: A line replaceable unit (LRU) is a box that can be removed and replaced on the flight line. The definition is practical, not electrical: the swap needs hand tools and a short test, no hangar and no recalibration of the whole aircraft. Each LRU has a part number, a connector list and a self-test that runs when power is applied.

Hold four things in view for any avionics layout: sensors (air data probes, inertial measurement units), computers (the boxes that process), data buses (the wires or fibres that carry messages) and displays (what the crew sees). Power and cooling cut across all four; see Unit 3 for generation, distribution, packaging and cooling.

In a federated architecture each LRU owns exactly one function. The air data computer computes airspeed and altitude. The inertial reference unit gives attitude and heading. The autopilot computer moves the control surfaces. Signals travel on dedicated point-to-point wires between boxes, so each function has its own private path.

items: Fault isolation is simple: a fault leads to one box, the box is swapped, the aircraft flies.
Each box is certified on its own, with no shared software to argue about.
Cost: weight, volume, power and connector count multiply with every added function.
Spares: many part numbers must be stocked at every station on the network.

sections.h3: IMA: shared cabinets, modules and partitions

blocks.text: Integrated modular avionics (IMA) replaces many single-function boxes with a few cabinets. A cabinet holds modules — processor modules, input/output modules and power supply modules — that plug into a backplane, a printed board carrying power and data between them. The wiring inside the cabinet is fixed; the function lives in software loaded onto a module.

Each function runs as a partition. ARINC 653 is the standard that defines this arrangement: a partition gets a fixed time slot on the processor and its own memory area, so one function cannot read another's data or take its processor time. Software partitioning detail belongs to Chapter 4.9.

Redundancy does not disappear. A cabinet can hold a standby processor module; if the active module fails, the standby takes the partition over. Because the hardware is now shared, a shared failure is possible, so designers add redundancy rather than remove it. The modules feed the cockpit through switched buses such as AFDX (Chapter 4.8).
Some syllabi call the same idea integrated avionics. The name covers the whole aircraft-level change: shared cabinets, shared buses and shared displays.

sections.h3: BITE, maintenance data and the trade-off

blocks.text: Every LRU and every IMA module carries built-in test equipment (BITE). BITE is circuitry and software inside the box that injects test signals and checks the response. It runs at power-up, continuously in flight, and on command from a maintenance panel. It stores fault codes in non-volatile memory.

Those codes travel over a data bus to a central maintenance computer, then to a maintenance recorder or a ground link. A technician on the apron reads them and goes straight to the suspect box, so a fault is found in minutes instead of hours of probing. This matters on a tight turnaround, where a delay in finding the fault costs the schedule.

blocks.where: m<sub>fed</sub> is the mass of one replaced federated LRU in kg, summed over all replaced units; m<sub>IMA</sub> is the total mass of the cabinet with its modules in kg; Δm is the mass saved in kg. The same subtraction in watts gives the power saved.

items: Mass, volume, power and connector count fall, because there are fewer boxes and fewer wires.
Wiring falls again when shared buses replace point-to-point links.
Certification work rises: every hosted function must be shown to be isolated from its neighbours.
The shared cabinet is a common point, so its failure must be covered by redundancy.

examples.question: An aircraft carries 8 federated LRUs, each of mass 2 kg and drawing 40 W. An IMA cabinet replaces all eight with 3 modules whose total mass is 5 kg and total draw is 90 W. Find the mass saved and the power saved, and express each saving as a percentage of the federated figure.
steps: Mass saved Δm = 16 kg − 5 kg = 11 kg.
Power saved ΔP = 320 W − 90 W = 230 W.
Mass saving as a percentage = (11 kg ÷ 16 kg) × 100 = 68.75 %.
Power saving as a percentage = (230 W ÷ 320 W) × 100 = 71.875 %.
examples.answer: 11 kg of mass and 230 W of power are saved, which is 68.75 % of the federated mass and 71.875 % of the federated power.
examples.check:
mass_fed_kg = 8 * 2
mass_ima_kg = 5
power_fed_w = 8 * 40
power_ima_w = 90

power_saved_w = power_fed_w - power_ima_w
mass_saved_pct = 100 * mass_saved_kg / mass_fed_kg
power_saved_pct = 100 * power_saved_w / power_fed_w

traps: IMA does not remove redundancy. Shared hardware makes a common failure possible, so designers add standby modules; an answer that says IMA saves weight by deleting duplicate boxes is wrong.
An LRU is the box, not a part inside it. A relay or a pressure switch inside a black box is not an LRU; the line replaceable unit is the box the technician unbolts.
BITE tests the unit it sits in and reports codes. It does not repair anything and it does not prove the whole system healthy, because the fault may lie in wiring or in a neighbour.
ARINC 653 is a software partitioning standard, not a bus standard. Do not confuse it with ARINC 429 or 664, which describe how bits travel on the wire.
Federated architecture is not obsolete. Light aircraft, helicopters and many military types still use it because its certification path is short and its fault isolation is obvious.

quiz.q: Define a line replaceable unit and state the property that makes it one.
quiz.a: An LRU is a box that can be removed and replaced on the flight line using hand tools and a short self-test, without a hangar visit or full aircraft recalibration. The property is line replaceability, not size or function.

quiz.q: What does BITE stand for, and name its three operating modes.
quiz.a: Built-in test equipment. The modes are power-up BITE, continuous (in-flight) BITE and initiated (command) BITE from the maintenance panel.

quiz.q: Why does a federated architecture multiply weight, connectors and part numbers as functions are added?
quiz.a: Each new function arrives as its own LRU with its own power supply, housing, cooling path and point-to-point wiring to its sensors and displays. Nothing is shared, so mass, connector count and spare part numbers grow in step with the number of functions. Each box also needs its own certification evidence.

quiz.q: Explain how ARINC 653 allows two functions to share one processor without interfering.
quiz.a: Each function runs as a partition. The partition gets a fixed time slot on the processor, enforced by a scheduler, and its own memory area, enforced by memory protection. A partition that misbehaves cannot read another's data and cannot take more than its slot, so timing and data are both protected.

quiz.q: Six federated LRUs, each of mass 3 kg and drawing 30 W, are replaced by one IMA cabinet of mass 4 kg drawing 70 W. Find the mass and power saved.
quiz.a: Federated mass = 6 × 3 = 18 kg; mass saved = 18 − 4 = 14 kg. Federated power = 6 × 30 = 180 W; power saved = 180 − 70 = 110 W.

quiz.q: Why does a shared IMA cabinet need more redundancy, not less, than a federated layout?
quiz.a: In a federated layout a single box failure removes one function only. In a cabinet, one failed module or one failed backplane can remove several functions at once, so the failure is common-mode. The architecture must therefore replicate modules and often replicate cabinets, and route partitions to a standby, so the number of failure paths is greater even though the number of boxes is smaller.

quiz.q: BITE reports no fault, yet the crew reports a wrong reading on a display. Give two reasons why the report and the reading can disagree.
quiz.a: First, BITE tests the unit it lives in and its own interfaces, so a fault in the wiring, a connector or a neighbouring unit is invisible to it. Second, BITE compares against stored limits and may pass a unit that is inside tolerance but drifting, or it may not test the specific path the crew uses, such as a scaling table applied downstream.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern wide-body aircraft carry the IMA idea further: remote data concentrators sit near the sensors and send digital words to the cabinet, replacing long analogue runs. Research and standards work now pushes open architectures, where a module from one supplier can host software from another under a published interface contract, and military programmes use similar modular concepts. Search next for ARINC 653, ARINC 664 part 7, remote data concentrators and open avionics architecture, and compare how the same partitioning idea appears in each.
